title: Write a `Supplier<Employee>` that creates a default employee.
shortTitle: Write a Supplier<Employee> that creates a default employee
keyPoints: Supplier<T> takes no input and returns a value from its get() method
Laziness is the key benefit: the object is created only when get() is called
orElseGet(supplier) calls the supplier only when the Optional is empty (lazy)
orElse(value) always evaluates its argument even when the Optional has a value (eager)
Stream.generate(supplier) produces an infinite stream of values from a supplier
Use Supplier to defer expensive or side-effecting construction

s1_definition.oneliner: Supplier<Employee> takes nothing and returns a fresh Employee from get(): perfect for lazy defaults.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Supplier<T>** has a single `get()` method taking no input and returning a value.
- **Laziness**: the object is built only when `get()` is called, not when the Supplier is defined.
- **orElseGet(supplier)** defers construction to the empty case.
- **orElse(value)** eagerly evaluates the default even when unused.
- **Stream.generate(supplier)** produces values on demand.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India keeps a stamp that prints a blank default employee form on demand. Whenever she needs one, she presses the stamp. No inputs needed, out comes a fresh default.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Supplier<Employee>  () -> new Employee("UNKNOWN")

  Not called yet → no object created

  Optional.empty()
       │
       │  .orElseGet(supplier)
       │  Optional is empty → call supplier.get()
       ▼
  new Employee("UNKNOWN")  ← created on demand

  Optional.of(existing)
       │
       │  .orElseGet(supplier)
       │  Optional has value → supplier NOT called
       ▼
  existing  ← supplier was never invoked
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Supplier is a functional interface with a no-argument get() method that returns a value. Its key benefit is laziness: the value is created only when get() is called, not when the Supplier is defined.

This is why orElseGet(supplier) is better than orElse(value) when the default is expensive: orElse always evaluates its argument, while orElseGet calls the supplier only when the Optional is empty. At the National Bank of India, the account lookup used orElseGet to avoid constructing a default employee object on every successful find.

Supplier is also the factory behind Stream.generate for on-demand value production and behind computeIfAbsent for lazy map population.

Remember one sentence: Supplier defers construction to when get() is called, and orElseGet uses that laziness to avoid building a default when the Optional already has a value.
